verses.note: Genesis presents the serpent as a creature, not a god, and does not name a power behind it. Later Scripture identifies the tempter with the devil, calling him the ancient serpent (Revelation 12:9) and warning that he deceived Eve by his cunning (2 Corinthians 11:3).

On the oldest Jewish reading, followed by many early Christian writers, the sons of God are angelic beings who left their proper place. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 are often read as alluding to this. Others hold that angels cannot marry (Matthew 22:30) and read the phrase of human rulers or of Seth's line. Christians hold all three views.

The angel of the LORD is distinct from the LORD in name yet speaks as the LORD himself (verse 10) and is identified with him (verse 13). Interpreters have understood him as a created messenger bearing God's full authority, as a direct appearance of God, or, as many in the early church held, as the Son before his incarnation.

Two of the visitors are called angels in 19:1, and they eat. Scripture does not explain how heavenly messengers take human form and share a meal. It simply shows God stooping to meet Abraham at his own table, which is why Hebrews 13:2 can urge hospitality as a place where heavenly visitors may be met.
The same messengers who eat at Abraham's table carry out judgment on Sodom. Angels in Scripture are God's servants for rescue and for judgment alike (Hebrews 1:14, Revelation 16:1).

The angel of God speaks as God, promising in the first person, "I will make him into a great nation". In Genesis this messenger often speaks with God's own voice (16:10, 22:11-12), which is why interpreters ask whether he is a created messenger or a form of God's own presence.

The angel of the LORD speaks in God's first person ("from me"), as in Genesis 16:10 and 21:18. Many Christian interpreters have seen in this figure an appearance of God himself, some identifying him with the Son before the incarnation; others regard him as a messenger who speaks with his sender's full authority. The text does not settle it.
The angel here is never seen. His work is described only by its results, a road that goes right, which is how Scripture often presents the unseen help of God's messengers (Exodus 23:20, Psalm 91:11).

The angels are shown at work, passing between heaven and earth, which fits the Bible's picture of them as God's servants sent on errands for those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). Jacob sees that the world he fled into is not left to itself.

The angels say nothing and do nothing but meet Jacob. Their presence is itself the message: the God who promised at Bethel to keep him on the way out is keeping him on the way back, and Jacob names the place for God's camp before he names anything for his own fear.

Jacob identifies the angel with the God who shepherded him. Many church fathers, including Justin Martyr, read such appearances of the angel of the LORD as the Son of God before the incarnation; others, both ancient and modern, read the angel as a created messenger through whom God acts and speaks. The verse itself joins the angel to God by the singular verb, without explaining how.

The angel of the LORD appears in verse 2, but in verse 4 it is God who speaks from the bush and says ‘I am the God of your father’. The Old Testament often blurs the line this way (Genesis 16:7-13; Judges 13:21-22). Some interpreters understand the angel as a messenger who speaks with God's full authority; others see a direct appearance of God; and many early Christian writers identified the angel of the LORD with the Son before his incarnation. The text itself stresses that in meeting the angel Moses met God.

The thousands who serve and the myriads who stand are the heavenly host, the angels who attend God's throne (Deuteronomy 33:2; Psalm 68:17). Revelation 5:11 echoes the numbers in its vision of the angels around the throne and the Lamb.

The angel's work is to speak God's word at the decisive moment and then disappear. Angels in Matthew serve the story of Jesus at its beginning and its end; they announce and do not replace the obedience of the people they address.

The angels the devil wanted Jesus to summon by a leap come on the Father's initiative once the test is over. The verse presents angels as servants of the Son, ready at his Father's command (26:53), and it answers Psalm 91's promise in the psalm's own way: protection given, not extracted.

The demons are expelled by speech alone. Matthew's addition of ‘with a word’ puts spiritual powers in the same category as the sickness of the centurion's servant: both yield to the word of Jesus, which shows the demons as real but subordinate.

The demons know who Jesus is and know their end; their knowledge is accurate and useless to them. The verse teaches that evil powers are real, personal in their speech, and already doomed, and that the coming of Jesus brings their judgment forward into the present.
A single word, ‘Go’, is enough. The demons can ask but cannot act without leave, which is the picture of evil powers the Bible gives from Job 1 onward: destructive, but on a leash held by God.

The accusation assumes a real kingdom of demons with a ruler; the Pharisees do not deny Jesus' power over it, only its source. Jesus will answer that a kingdom divided cannot stand and that his exorcisms mean the strong man is being bound (12:25-29).
Angels serve Jesus in the wilderness. Scripture presents them as ministering spirits sent to serve (Hebrews 1:14), and here their service marks Jesus as the one God upholds.

The verse names Satan as an active opponent of the word, working at the moment of hearing. Scripture treats unbelief as more than an intellectual failure; there is an enemy who wants the word forgotten (compare 2 Corinthians 4:4).
The spirits are many and organized, yet they cannot act without Jesus' permission. The verses picture evil as real and powerful but wholly subject to him.

The demons are allowed to go where they ask, and what they enter they destroy. The verse shows the character of evil: it does not merely occupy but ruins, and it has no life of its own apart from what it can possess.
The angels serve the Son of Man as they serve God, a detail that places Jesus above them (Mark 8:38, Hebrews 1:6).

The angel's role is to interpret, not to perform. He does not raise Jesus or display him; he announces what God has done and sends the women on. In Scripture angels serve God's word to people, and the proper response is fear before God, not attention to the messenger.
The angel is ‘of the Lord’, a messenger defined wholly by the one who sends him. In Luke angels announce and interpret (1:26, 2:9, 24:4) but never become the center of the story.
The demons know who Jesus is and fear destruction. Their recognition is true in content and hostile in intent, which is why Jesus refuses their testimony (4:35, 41).

Luke speaks of evil spirits and illnesses side by side but keeps them distinct, as he does throughout (4:40-41, 6:18, 7:21). Deliverance from demonic power is part of what the kingdom brings, and those who were freed become the King's followers.

The devil is presented as an active opponent of the word, working at the moment of hearing. Scripture does not make him the only reason a hearer fails; the next soils locate the danger in shallowness and distraction. But it does treat the contest over the word as spiritual.

The unclean spirits know who Jesus is and fear him, which is recognition without trust (compare James 2:19). The powers that enslave people are not rivals to Jesus; they plead with him and cannot resist him.

Satan appears as a real power with a position that can be lost. The New Testament speaks of his defeat as begun in Jesus' ministry, decisive at the cross (John 12:31), and final at the end (Revelation 20:10).

The opponents do not deny that something supernatural has happened; they dispute its source. The Gospels assume a world of spiritual powers hostile to God, and the question they press is whose power is at work in Jesus.

Angels are witnesses of what God does in human lives. Scripture elsewhere pictures them attending to the salvation of God's people (1 Peter 1:12, Hebrews 1:14); here they stand in the presence where heaven's joy over one person is expressed.

Jesus affirms the existence of angels against the Sadducees and uses them as the point of comparison for the risen: deathless beings. The risen do not become angels; they are like them in not dying, and they remain human, called sons of God.

As angels served Jesus after the testing in the wilderness (Matthew 4:11, Mark 1:13), an angel strengthens him at the beginning of the final trial. The angel does not take the cup away; he strengthens Jesus to drink it, which is the pattern of help Scripture most often describes.

If tou ponērou is masculine, as the BSB takes it, Jesus names the devil as the enemy from whom the disciples need guarding, the ruler of this world of 12:31 and 16:11. 1 John uses the same term for the evil one whom the young men have overcome and who cannot touch the one born of God (1 John 2:13-14, 5:18).
Angels, rulers, and powers are real in Paul's world, but they are creatures. The verse sets every spiritual power, good or hostile, beneath the love of God in Christ.
Jewish tradition honored angels as present at Sinai. Paul uses the tradition to show the law's indirectness: it came through intermediaries, while the promise came from God himself.

The powers are real in Paul's view (6:12 calls them rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms), but they are subject to Christ. Believers need not fear or placate them, since the one they belong to reigns over them all.
Angelic and spiritual powers are creatures of Christ. Whatever rank they hold, they owe their existence to him, which is why the letter warns against the worship of angels (2:18).

Angels are creatures and servants whose form God can change. The contrast with the Son's eternal throne (verse 8) and unchanging being (verse 12) is the point: however glorious, they belong to the created order.

Angels serve God by serving his people. The verse supports the church's teaching on the ministry of angels, while its setting insists they are servants, not objects of devotion. Whether each believer has a particular guardian angel, a view held by many church fathers and in Catholic and Orthodox piety, the verse does not say.

The angels fight on God's side, and their victory is real but derivative. The verse shows the unseen dimension of the church's conflict without making angels the center; the hymn that follows credits the victory to the blood of the Lamb.
